title: Bombay High Court Bars Sanjay Dutt's Pune Nightclub From Playing Music Without License
excerpt: The court restrained Dutt's Ballr nightclub from using copyrighted songs after Phonographic Performance Limited filed a copyright infringement suit.
body:
• The Bombay High Court has restrained Sanjay Dutt's Ballr nightclub in Pune from playing copyrighted music without proper authorization from PPL India
  • Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL), which controls public performance rights for over 3 million sound recordings, filed the copyright infringement action
  • The ruling is part of a broader crackdown by PPL India against venues across Maharashtra that play music without valid licenses
  • Dutt, one of Bollywood's biggest stars, has faced multiple legal entanglements over the years alongside his acting career

The Bombay High Court has restrained actor Sanjay Dutt's Ballr nightclub in Pune from playing copyrighted songs without obtaining proper authorization, in a ruling that underscores the growing legal enforcement of music licensing in India's entertainment venues.

The order came after Phonographic Performance Limited (PPL India), the country's largest music licensing body, filed a copyright infringement suit against the nightclub. PPL India controls the public performance rights for over 3 million domestic and international sound recordings across more than 360 music labels, including T-Series, Sony Music, Universal Music, and Saregama.

Copyright Enforcement Tightens Across Maharashtra

The ruling against Ballr is not an isolated case. PPL India has been aggressively pursuing venues across Maharashtra and beyond that play copyrighted music without valid licenses. Earlier this year, the Bombay High Court issued a similar injunction against restaurant chains operating 94 outlets, restraining them from playing PPL-controlled music without authorization.

In a related case, the court issued bailable warrants against the proprietors of Grand Arsh for failing to comply with judicial directions in a contempt proceeding, signaling that courts are taking a harder line on repeat offenders.

The Bombay High Court has consistently upheld that commercial establishments — including hotels, restaurants, pubs, clubs, and bars — cannot use copyright-protected sound recordings without obtaining a valid public performance license from the rights holder. The Copyright Act, 1957 exposes infringers to both civil and potential criminal liability.

Sanjay Dutt's Business Ventures

Sanjay Dutt, 67, remains one of Bollywood's most prominent actors, known for films spanning four decades from the Munna Bhai series to recent action roles. Beyond acting, Dutt has diversified into business ventures including nightlife establishments and a whisky brand. In a separate recent case, the Delhi High Court restrained a Dutt-backed company, Cartel Bros, from using the 'Godfather' trademark to sell whisky after rival Devans Modern Breweries argued the mark had acquired substantial goodwill over four decades.

What This Means for Venues

The ruling serves as a warning to entertainment venues across India. PPL India has stated that any establishment communicating copyrighted sound recordings to the public — through any medium — must obtain a valid public performance license before doing so. Failure to comply constitutes infringement under the Copyright Act and can result in monetary penalties, seizure of equipment, and even criminal prosecution.

For nightclub and restaurant operators, the cost of a PPL license is typically a small fraction of operating expenses, but enforcement has historically been lax. The recent string of Bombay High Court orders suggests that era is ending.
